A rapidly absorbed short-acting SSRI, dapoxetine, is un- der development specifically for on-demand treatment of premature ejaculation. Topical anaesthetics, such as lido- caine/prilocaine cream, have been applied to the penis to delay ejaculation.1-3 Disadvantages of this therapy include loss of erection due to numbness associated with pro- longed application, and numbness in the partner caused by residual topical anaesthetic.1,3 Available commercial prep- arations intended for such use include benzocaine gels and lidocaine sprays. Sildenafil, a phosphodiesterase type-5 in- hibitor used for erectile dysfunction, has also been tried with some success;1 however, some consider that such drugs should only be used in patients with co-morbid erec- tile dysfunction.3 1. Prostatitis The term prostatitis is used to describe several clinical syn- dromes, including well-defined bacterial infections of the prostate gland, poorly-defined chronic pelvic pain, and asymptomatic inflammation of the prostate. Prostatitis is relatively common as a urological diagnosis, with about 30% of men having such symptoms at some time in their life.1 The US National Institutes of Health classification system1 for prostatitis consists of categories: • I: acute bacterial prostatitis • II: chronic bacterial prostatitis • III: chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome (subdivided into IIIA inflammatory and IIIB non- inflammatory) • IV: asymptomatic inflammatory prostatitis Acute bacterial prostatitis (category I) is most often due to Gram-negative pathogens, particularly Escherichia coli and other enterobacteriaceae. Symptoms include fever, chills, malaise and myalgia, with rectal, low back, or peri- neal pain. There is often bacteriuria with frequent and ur- gent dysuria. The prostate is enlarged, tender, and warm.1,2 Chronic bacterial prostatitis (category II) is relatively rare, and may develop from acute bacterial prostatitis in some men.
